name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 22 September 1973

clue.text: Harbour needs bush for nursery merry-go-round

blocks.note: first meaning: the prefabricated floating harbours towed to Normandy for D-Day in 1944
second meaning: the bush children circle in the rhyme 'Here we go round the ... bush'

explanation.surface: A port wants some shrubbery for a children's ring game.
explanation.walkthrough: The Second World War artificial harbours off Normandy shared their code name with the bush in the nursery rhyme 'Here we go round the mulberry bush'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mulberry was the code name of the portable wartime harbours, and the nursery rhyme's dancers circle a mulberry bush.

clue.text: Its first runner was late arriving in Athens

definitions.text: Its first runner was late arriving in Athens

blocks.clueFragment: Its first runner was late arriving
blocks.note: surface reading: the first competitor came in behind time
setter's reading: late as in dead, since the messenger died on reaching Athens

explanation.walkthrough: 'Late' looks like 'tardy' but means deceased: legend says the messenger collapsed and died after delivering news of victory.
explanation.definitionFit: The long-distance race commemorates the messenger who ran from the battlefield at Marathon to Athens.

clue.text: Country variety of mail horse

definitions.note: the answer is a county, standing for rural country

indicators.note: a variety is a different form, so these letters take on another arrangement

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A rural breed of the horse that once pulled mail coaches.
explanation.walkthrough: LOAMSHIRE is the made-up English county used in novels and plays to stand for any rural shire.
explanation.definitionFit: Loamshire is the fictional county of English writing, a byword for the farming countryside.

clue.text: Race spirit discernible in a Dorset hostelry

indicators.note: something discernible inside the following words can be seen sitting within them

blocks.note: straddles the end of the county and the start of the inn

explanation.surface: The atmosphere of horse racing can be felt in a West Country pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Race spirit' suggests drink at a racecourse, but it is the characteristic spirit of a people. Dorset is a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: An ethos is the characteristic spirit or values of a people or community.

clue.text: Line of travel included in the drill

indicators.note: included means taken inside, so the little word goes within the path

blocks.note: a route is a line of travel
taken as written

explanation.surface: A marching route is part of the parade-ground exercise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is not a link here but the letters inserted: ROUT(IN)E.
explanation.definitionFit: 'The drill' is idiom for the usual procedure, the established order of doing things.

clue.text: High flyer ditched through overheating

blocks.note: surface reading: an ambitious pilot forced down into the sea
setter's reading: the boy of Greek myth whose wax wings melted when he flew too near the sun

explanation.surface: An aircraft ditches in the sea after its engine overheats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ditched' is aviation slang for landing on water, which is exactly what happened when the sun melted the wax of the mythical wings.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend Icarus flew too close to the sun, his wings melted and he fell into the sea.

clue.text: When Henry V speaks "the air, a libertine, ' is still"

definitions.text: When Henry V speaks "the air, a libertine, ' is still

blocks.note: the setting: the Archbishop of Canterbury praising the new king in Henry V, Act 1 Scene 1
the quotation with one word missing, the adjective describing the libertine

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank: the newspaper text lost the gap marker. Shakespeare wrote 'The air, a charter'd libertine, is still', the answer spelt out in full.
explanation.definitionFit: Chartered means licensed or privileged, so the air is pictured as a free spirit with a royal licence to roam.

clue.text: Sharp girl begins to make an instrument

indicators.note: only the start of the name is kept, the tail being cut away

blocks.note: Becky Sharp, the heroine of Thackeray's Vanity Fair, is Rebecca in full

explanation.surface: A clever young woman starts building a musical instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sharp' looks like an adjective for clever or a musical note, but it is Becky Sharp's surname. The first five letters of her full name give REBEC.
explanation.definitionFit: A rebec is a medieval bowed string instrument, an ancestor of the fiddle.

clue.text: Look pleased about one literary comparison

indicators.note: about means around, so the facial expression goes round the numeral

blocks.note: to smile is to look pleased
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone is delighted by a particular figure of speech.
explanation.walkthrough: S(I)MILE.
explanation.definitionFit: A simile is a figure of speech comparing two things using 'like' or 'as'.

clue.text: Ornament to be put on top of a ship

blocks.note: taken as written
the deck is the part of a ship that forms its top surface

explanation.surface: A decoration is to be fitted on top of a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, one piece put on top of another comes before it. 'Ornament' looks like a noun but works as a verb, to decorate.
explanation.definitionFit: To bedeck is to decorate or adorn, the verb sense of ornament.

clue.text: By the way Christ Church caters for travellers

definitions.note: a description of what the place does rather than a noun for it

blocks.note: a way is a road
Christ Church, Oxford, is known to its members as 'the House'

explanation.surface: An Oxford college runs a sideline feeding passing tourists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By the way' reads as a throwaway aside, but 'the way' is wordplay. Christ Church is the Oxford college traditionally called the House.
explanation.definitionFit: A roadhouse is an inn or restaurant on a main road serving meals and drinks to motorists.

clue.text: It holds family records (revolutionary or not)

definitions.text: It holds family records (revolutionary or not)

blocks.note: surface reading: a register or archive of births and marriages
setter's reading: the book of family photographs, or a set of gramophone discs that spin as they play

explanation.surface: A book of family history, with a hint at radical politics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' sounds political, but it means turning on a turntable: the word covers both a photograph book and a long-playing record.
explanation.definitionFit: An album holds family snapshots, and an album is also a collection of musical recordings on spinning discs.

clue.text: Ivory from Monmouthshire shire river town in a back-street

definitions.note: a mass noun standing for the plural answer

indicators.note: going back means the abbreviation for street is read from its end
the town is placed in the middle of the turned street

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation for street
Usk is both a river and a small town in Monmouthshire

explanation.surface: Ivory turning up down a side alley in a Welsh border town.
explanation.walkthrough: The newspaper text repeats 'shire', a printing slip. Monmouthshire is a county in south-east Wales, through which the River Usk runs.
explanation.definitionFit: Elephant tusks are the source of ivory, so the material stands for the teeth themselves.

clue.text: I study it backwards, state it's the same

indicators.note: the word it is to be read from its last letter to its first

blocks.note: taken as written
a den is a private study
the little word turned round
an abbreviation for the US state of California

explanation.surface: Someone notices that a phrase reads the same reversed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a palindrome, but only the little word 'it' is turned round. CAL is a standard abbreviation for California.
explanation.definitionFit: Identical things are exactly alike, which is what being the same means.

clue.text: Love cereal, if put inside the mouth

indicators.note: these words ask for the little conditional word to be placed within the grain

blocks.note: love is nil in tennis, the round zero
rice is a cereal grain
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who loves cereal and hopes it can be spooned into their mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love' as zero comes from tennis scoring. The comma splits the clue so that 'if' looks like a conjunction rather than letters to insert.
explanation.definitionFit: An orifice is an opening of the body, and the mouth is the most familiar example.

clue.text: Fly from one Munich imbroglio

indicators.note: an imbroglio is a confused tangle, so these letters are muddled up

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone escapes from a tangled affair in Munich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly' looks like the verb 'flee', but it is the insect.
explanation.definitionFit: The ichneumon fly is a parasitic wasp-like insect that lays its eggs in caterpillars.

clue.text: Dam where Kipling's snake swallowed a bone

indicators.note: a snake swallowing something takes it whole into its body

blocks.note: Kaa is the python in Kipling's The Jungle Book
a rib is a bone

explanation.surface: At a reservoir, the python from The Jungle Book gulps down a bone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dam' could be a mother animal, but here it is a real dam, named for the gorge it blocks.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kariba Dam on the Zambezi, between Zambia and Rhodesia, was one of the largest hydroelectric dams of its day.

clue.text: Stick on soles making it hard to walk?

definitions.text: Stick on soles making it hard to walk?

blocks.note: surface reading: gluing new soles onto shoes
setter's reading: a cane beaten on the soles of the feet, an old punishment that leaves the victim unable to walk

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick' looks like the verb 'glue' but is a noun, the cane used in this eastern punishment.
explanation.definitionFit: The bastinado is a punishment of beating the soles of the feet with a cane, which leaves walking painful.

clue.text: Sicily's mountain - climb takes in one place for a liqueur

indicators.note: in a down clue, climbing means reading upwards, so the mountain's letters run backwards
taking in means holding something inside, so the turned mountain surrounds the rest

blocks.note: Etna is the volcano on Sicily
the Roman numeral for one
to set something is to place it

explanation.surface: A climber on Etna stops at a spot to enjoy a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Place' is a verb here, to set down, not a noun for a location.
explanation.definitionFit: Anisette is a sweet liqueur flavoured with aniseed.

clue.text: A way of acting

blocks.note: surface reading: a manner of behaving or a procedure
setter's reading: the Stanislavski-based stage technique of Brando and the Actors Studio

explanation.walkthrough: Read plainly it means any procedure; read theatrically it names the style in which actors live their roles.
explanation.definitionFit: A method is a way of doing something, and the Method is a famous school of stage and screen acting.

clue.text: Tell someone the way that is straight

blocks.note: first meaning: to give someone directions
second meaning: going by the shortest line, without deviation

explanation.surface: Giving someone directions that are simple and plain.
explanation.definitionFit: To direct someone is to show them the way, and a direct route or answer is a straight one.

clue.text: A learned cleric has one boy. Joseph

blocks.note: taken as written
a Doctor of Divinity, a learned degree held by clergy
the Roman numeral for one
a son is a boy

explanation.surface: A scholarly clergyman has a single child, a boy named Joseph.
explanation.walkthrough: The full stop makes 'Joseph' look like the boy's name, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Addison was the eighteenth-century essayist who co-founded The Spectator, so his first name points to the surname.

clue.text: Slander Parsees perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the word is only one possible arrangement of its letters

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange; Parsees are Zoroastrians of Indian descent

explanation.surface: A defamatory remark about a religious community.
explanation.walkthrough: The newspaper text reads 'Parsecs', but the letters must be PARSEES, the Zoroastrian community of India.
explanation.definitionFit: To asperse is to attack someone's reputation with damaging claims, which is what slander does.

clue.text: A crazy one? Point to Gaul's romantic hero

blocks.note: taken as written
mad means crazy
the Roman numeral for one
south, a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Pointing out a madman as the hero of a French romance.
explanation.walkthrough: Amadis of Gaul is the knight of a sixteenth-century Spanish chivalric romance, the book that turned Don Quixote's head.
explanation.definitionFit: Amadis is the title hero of the prose romance Amadis of Gaul, a model of the knight-errant.

clue.text: Play catching a conscience — or vermin?

definitions.text: Play catching a conscience — or vermin?

blocks.note: Hamlet's play within the play, staged so that 'the play's the thing wherein I'll catch the conscience of the king'
the same name for a household device that catches small rodents

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a drama is meant to trap a guilty mind or pests.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet names his play after a household trap; the name is also the title of Agatha Christie's long-running London play.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet names the play he stages before Claudius after a rodent trap, and such a device literally catches vermin.

clue.text: Total put in circulation

blocks.note: first meaning: complete, absolute, as in a total fool
second meaning: to pass coins or notes, especially forged ones, into use

explanation.surface: A sum of money is released into the economy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Total' looks like a noun for a sum, but it is the adjective meaning complete.
explanation.definitionFit: Utter means complete or absolute, and to utter counterfeit money is the legal term for passing it.

clue.text: Booked as master carpenter

blocks.note: first meaning: Mr ..., the schoolmaster of James Hilton's novel Goodbye, Mr ...
second meaning: the traditional nickname for a ship's carpenter

explanation.surface: Someone is hired as a senior woodworker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Booked' sounds like being hired, but it means appearing in a book. Calling a ship's carpenter 'Chips' is old naval slang.
explanation.definitionFit: The title schoolmaster of Hilton's book bears this name, and ship's carpenters were nicknamed after their wood shavings.

clue.text: It's near the cathedral

blocks.note: surface reading: something situated nearby
setter's reading: the walled precinct of clergy houses around a cathedral, whose name is also an adjective for nearby

explanation.walkthrough: The precinct round an English cathedral, where the clergy live, shares its name with the adjective for nearby.
explanation.definitionFit: A cathedral's precinct is called by a word that also means nearby, so the area beside it is both.

clue.text: The line we're given?

blocks.note: surface reading: an actor's line, or the official story handed out
setter's reading: a surveyor's reference line, whose name is Latin for 'something given'

explanation.walkthrough: The Latin word for 'given' names a fixed reference line from which surveyors measure heights.
explanation.definitionFit: A datum is literally a thing given, and a datum line is the baseline from which levels are measured.

clue.text: Troops can be destroyed by St Elmo's fire

indicators.note: something destroyed is broken up, so these letters lose their order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Soldiers could be wiped out by an eerie electrical glow.
explanation.definitionFit: A corposant is the glowing electrical discharge seen on masts in stormy weather, also called St Elmo's fire.

clue.text: Something lyrical about a redhead's garment

indicators.note: about means going round, so the lyrical piece surrounds the rest

blocks.note: a song is set to lyrics
taken as written
the head, or first letter, of red

explanation.surface: A ballad written about a red-haired woman's dress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Redhead' looks like a person, but it is split into red plus its head. S(A R)ONG.
explanation.definitionFit: A sarong is a wraparound cloth garment worn round the waist in South-East Asia.

clue.text: Writer appears to' run away with her

blocks.note: a pen is an instrument that writes
to elope is to run away to marry

explanation.surface: An author seems to be running off with a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The stray apostrophe after 'to' is a printing blemish. The definition is the bare pronoun: the woman whose name the wordplay spells.
explanation.definitionFit: Penelope is a woman's name, so it can stand for the female pronoun, here the lady a suitor might run off with.
